title: Hello!
goal: Greet people at the right level of politeness, introduce yourself, ask how someone is, and say goodbye — while learning *a fi* (to be), a verb that changes for every person.
bekal: greet and say goodbye with *salut*, *bună ziua*, *pa*, and *la revedere*, each in its proper place
give your name with *mă cheamă…* and introduce others with *el este… / ea este…*
use all six forms of *a fi* and choose between *tu* and *dumneavoastră*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Prima zi la birou
dialogs.intro: It's Budi's first day at his new office in București. A colleague comes over to his desk. Near the end of the day, Andrei — Budi's flatmate — stops by to pick him up.

notes: **Cum te cheamă? is not "what is your name".** Literally it is "how does (one) call you?" — someone else is the doer, and you are just the target (*te*). That's why the verb doesn't change: *mă cheamă* (I'm called), *te cheamă* (you're called). To someone you address formally: *Cum vă cheamă?* There is also a more formal pair, *Cum te numești? — Mă numesc Budi*, which you'll often see on forms.

**Încântat or încântată — it follows the speaker.** Budi is a man, so *încântat*; Ioana is a woman, so *încântată*. If you don't want to choose, use *Îmi pare bine* like Andrei: it's the same for everyone.

**Ce mai faci? literally means "what else are you doing?"** The little word *mai* is what turns an ordinary question into "how are you". The standard answer is *Bine, mulțumesc*; other options: *Foarte bine* (very well) and *Așa și așa* (so-so). To someone you address formally: *Ce mai faceți?*

**Ea este Ioana — introductions use *el* and *ea* (he/she), not "this".** For a man: *El este Andrei, colegul meu*. Look at *colega mea*: "my" comes after the noun, and the noun gets the ending *-a*. That ending is the definite article; it gets fitted in units 3 and 4 — for now, learn the phrase whole.

**Budi is still too formal.** *La revedere* goes with *bună ziua*, while friends say goodbye with *pa*. Ioana doesn't correct him — she just answers *Pa!*, and that's how Romanians tell you you can relax.

grammars.title: Subject pronouns and a fi — the "to be" you can't skip
body: Like English, Romanian needs its verb "to be": *Sunt student* = I am a student. The difference is that the verb changes for every person, and the pronoun usually disappears. Learn all six forms until they come out on their own.
after: **The pronoun is often dropped.** The verb ending already holds the subject, so *Sunt student* can only mean "I'm a student". *Eu* and *tu* are used only to **emphasize or contrast**: *Eu sunt Ioana* ("as for me, I'm Ioana"), *Și tu ești programatoare?* ("are you a programmer **too**?"). The one trap: *sunt* means both "I am" and "they are" — context tells you which.
***Este* and *e* mean the same.** *Este* is neater and safe anywhere; *e* is the short form you hear in conversation: *Ea e Ioana*. In this course the dialogues use *este* so the pattern stays clear.

***Ei* and *ele*.** *Ele* is used only when everyone is female; as soon as there's one man in the group, it becomes *ei*. Romanian also has no word "it" for things: objects too are called *el* or *ea*, because every noun has a gender. That's the story of unit 3.
**After *a fi*, jobs and nationalities take no article**: *Sunt student*, *Ești programatoare* — not *sunt un student*. Here English ("I'm a student") is the odd one out.

grammars.title: Tu versus dumneavoastră — two kinds of "you"
body: Romanian splits "you" the way French splits *tu* and *vous* — and the choice also changes the verb.

head: Form
Say it
Used with
Example
rows: one person, informal — friends, peers, family, children
one person, polite — strangers, bosses, older people

after: ***Dumneavoastră* always takes the *voi* verb form, even for just one person**: *Dumneavoastră sunteți doamna Popescu?* ("Are you Mrs. Popescu?"). So there's no new table to learn — just remember that polite = plural. In writing it's usually shortened to *dvs.*

**Rule of thumb: when in doubt, use *dumneavoastră*.** Being too polite to a friend just sounds stiff and is instantly forgiven; using *tu* with your landlady sounds rude. It's usually the Romanian who offers to switch first, with *Putem să ne tutuim?* ("Can we say *tu* to each other?"). In young offices in București, colleagues of the same age use *tu* from day one, like Ioana.

**Polite address uses *doamna* (Mrs./Ms.) and *domnul* (Mr.) + surname**: *Bună ziua, doamna Popescu!* The pairs are locked: **salut / pa + tu**, **bună ziua / la revedere + dumneavoastră**. If you remember just one thing from this page, remember those pairs.

sections.title: Greetings by time of day and closeness

blocks.text: Romanian greetings vary along two axes at once: the time of day, and how close you are to the person. This table covers both.

head: Română
Say it
When to use it
rows: Good day / good afternoon — all day, the safest polite greeting
Good night — only when parting to go to bed
Hi/bye — informal, typical of Transylvania; Andrei from Cluj uses it
See you tomorrow! / See you soon!
Have a nice day — said when parting

blocks.text: The one you'll need most is **bună ziua**: polite, never wrong, and good from morning to early evening. Romanians also say it to strangers when stepping into an elevator, a waiting room, or a small shop — silence feels cold. On the way out, say *la revedere* or *o zi bună*.

Why always *bună*, never *bun*? Because *ziua* (day), *dimineața* (morning), *seara* (evening), and *noaptea* (night) are all feminine nouns, and Romanian adjectives agree with the noun's gender. Notice the order too: *bună seara* is a greeting when you meet, while *noapte bună* — order reversed — is a wish when you part. One pronunciation note: *ea* is one quick glide from *e* to *a* within a single syllable, so *seara* is not "seh-ah-rah" but SYAH-rah.

blocks.title: Sărut mâna — "I kiss your hand"
items: Literally "(I) kiss the hand". It's a traditional respectful greeting from men to women, and from children to older people. The hand is almost never actually kissed; only the phrase remains.
You'll still hear it often, especially to older women. Budi can greet his landlady with *Sărut mâna, doamna Popescu!* — she'll be pleased. To Ioana? Don't; to a peer it sounds like a joke.

sections.title: Polite words that keep you afloat

blocks.text: These words aren't grammar homework — they're an emergency kit. Learn them whole now; understand how they're built later.

head: Română
Say it
English
rows: Please, come in; here you go; sorry, what was that?

blocks.text: *Te rog* and *vă rog* literally mean "I ask you" (informal / polite) — so the choice follows *tu* and *dumneavoastră*. In shops, cafés, and at ticket counters, always *vă rog*. It can go anywhere: *Vă rog, o cafea* or *O cafea, vă rog*.

*Cu plăcere* literally means "with pleasure", and it's the standard reply to *mulțumesc*. *Mulțumesc* itself is actually a verb — "I thank" — so if two of you are thanking, it becomes *mulțumim* ("we thank"). That *-esc* ending pattern arrives in unit 2.

*Poftim* is the most versatile word on this page. It means "please, come in" when inviting someone in, "here you go" when handing something over, and — with a questioning tone, *Poftim?* — "sorry, what was that?" when you didn't catch what someone said. The polite form is *poftiți*. *Problemă*, by the way, is the first of hundreds of Romanian words you already know from English.

items: Nice to meet you. (you're a man)
